newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Israel, PLO show few signs of flexibility.
newsitem.headline: Israel, PLO show few signs of flexibility.

text.p: A new cycle of Middle East violence enters its third week with Israel and the PLO showing few signs of flexibility.
Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said on Wednesday that Israel would not resume peacemaking as long as Palestinian bombs kept exploding.
Arabs insist the starting point for renewed peace talks should be a halt to Israeli construction of a new Jewish settlement in Arab East Jerusalem, which has touched off daily West Bank unrest.

All eyes have turned to Middle East peace sponsor Washington to put forward a new initiative. U.S. President Bill Clinton said on Tuesday he was "personally prepared to do anything I can" to put peace moves back on track.
Jordan's King Hussein discussed the troubled Middle East peace process with senior U.S. officials on Wednesday and pressed Washington to spark progress.

"The United States has a special and unique position of respect, of trust and of the confidence of all parties in our part of the world," he told reporters at the Pentagon before meeting U.S. Defence Secretary William Cohen.
Netanyahu told reporters on Wednesday: "The peace process can't be conducted while buses or cafes are exploding or while children are in danger of a terrorist blowing them up."

The Israeli leader spoke hours after a petrol bomb was thrown at an Israeli bus in the West Bank, causing it to overturn and injuring 11 soldiers. It was the third bombing Israel blamed on Palestinians in two days.
In the West Bank north of Jerusalem on Wednesday, Israeli troops dispersed Palestinian stone-throwers with tear gas and rubber bullets.
U.S. Secretary of State Madeleine Albright called Palestinian President Yasser Arafat twice on Wednesday to hear his views ahead of a hastily arranged visit by Netanyahu to Washington next week.
Arafat told Albright the crisis stemmed from Israel's East Jerusalem settlement.
"The Israeli settlement policy...places the entire peace process in real danger," the official Palestinian news agency Wafa quoted Arafat as telling Albright.
Palestinians complain the settlement pre-empts the results of final peace talks yet to come on the status of East Jerusalem, captured by Israel in 1967 and claimed by both sides.
Egypt, backing Arafat, called on Netanyahu to have the "courage" to back off over the East Jerusalem settlement.

"To save the peace process needs political statesmanship and courage. The practices and steps that have been taken in Jerusalem will have to be rolled back. This is the starting point for any effort to save the process," Egyptian Foreign Minister Amr Moussa said in Cairo.

Usama el-Baz, a senior political adviser to Egyptian President Hosni Mubarak, told journalists that the Middle East's nightmare -- the death of the peace process -- was possible if progress were interrupted for a long time.
"Consequences will be bleak for everybody," Baz said.
But Netanyahu said he would tell Clinton on Monday that halting the violence was the first priority.

"We will discuss the urgent need for the Palestinian Authority to start battling terrorism because without it we won't be able to move forward in the process," he said, adding that he did not expect U.S. pressure over his settlement policy.

U.S. State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns said in Washington on Wednesday the United States would like Arafat to clamp down on militants "who are bent on violence and terror and who are using that as a political tactic".
In the PLO-ruled Gaza Strip on Tuesday, two Palestinians were killed in explosions that Israel said were botched suicide bombings by the Islamic Jihad group aimed at Jewish children.

Jihad sources said on Wednesday the Palestinian Authority had arrested 30 of their activists in overnight raids. The group disavowed the two bombings, charging that Israel had staged them to divert attention from its settlement policy.
Israeli Foreign Minister David Levy vowed the Jewish state would not order its bulldozers to stop work on the East Jerusalem settlement.
"It is our right to build in Jerusalem. Period," he said.
